chunks: Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan, from Bakr ibn Salih, from al-Hasan ibn Sa'id, from al-Haytham ibn Abdillah, from Marwan ibn Sabbah, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Indeed, God created us and made our creation excellent; and He formed us and made our forms excellent; and He made us to be His Eye among His servants, and His Speaking Tongue among His creation, and His Extended Hand over His servants with kindness and mercy, and His Face through which one comes to Him, and His Door which guides to Him, and His Treasurers in His heaven and His earth.

Through us the trees bear fruit and the fruits ripen, and the rivers flow, and through us the rain of the heaven descends and the vegetation of the earth grows, and through our worship God is worshipped — and were it not for us, God would not be worshipped.

key_terms.خُزَّانَهُ: His Treasurers — the Imams as guardians of divine knowledge and blessings in heaven and earth
key_terms.عَيْنَهُ: His Eye — a metaphor for the Imam as God's watchful presence among humanity
key_terms.لِسَانَهُ النَّاطِقَ: His Speaking Tongue — the Imam as the articulate expression of divine speech and guidance
key_terms.وَجْهَهُ: His Face — the direction through which one approaches God; the Imam as the Qibla of divine proximity
key_terms.يَدَهُ الْمَبْسُوطَةَ: His Extended Hand — the Imam as the means by which divine mercy and kindness are dispensed

ai.seo_question: What is the cosmic status of the Imams in Shia Islam according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) articulates the metaphysical station of the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt in Shia theology, describing them as divine instruments through whom God's providence manifests in the cosmos. The Imam employs a series of vivid metaphors — eye, tongue, hand, face, door, and treasurers — to convey that the Imams serve as the intermediaries between God and creation. This hadith is a cornerstone of Imami cosmology: it presents the Imams not merely as religious guides but as the cosmic axis through which creation is sustained and through whose worship God is acknowledged, a teaching that would have been deeply significant to early Shia communities seeking to understand the ontological status of their Imams during a period of political suppression.
